opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. Memory is one of the most interesting and underexplored problems in agents right now.

Most of the work so far has been about making a single agent better within a single session: better reasoning, better tool use, longer context. But teams don't work that way. The most valuable knowledge in an organization isn't written down in one place. It's spread across conversations, code reviews, Slack threads, and the heads of people who've been around long enough to know why a decision was made. A new engineer takes months to absorb that. If every agent starts from zero each time, you're basically onboarding a new hire every morning.

What makes team-wide memory hard, and interesting, is that it isn't just a retrieval problem. Storing everything and doing search over it is easy. The hard questions are about curation. What's worth remembering? When does a memory become stale? If two people on the team gave the agent conflicting guidance, whose wins, and should the agent surface the conflict instead of silently picking one? There's also scoping: some things should be personal preferences, some team conventions, some org-wide policy. Humans navigate that intuitively, but you have to design it explicitly for agents.

Then there's trust. Shared memory means one person's correction can change how the agent behaves for everyone. That's powerful, because you get compounding learning across the team, but people need visibility into what the agent has learned and the ability to edit or delete it. Otherwise it feels like a black box slowly drifting.

The way I think about it, the real unlock isn't a smarter model in isolation. It's an agent that gets better the longer it works with your team, because it's accumulating the institutional knowledge that makes experienced people so effective. That compounding loop is what turns an agent from a tool into something closer to a colleague.

r001.rationale: The response says people need the ability to edit or delete learned memory, but it does not raise who is permitted to edit it as a design question.

r002.rationale: It discusses scoping memory into personal, team, and organization-wide categories and calls for visibility, but does not ask who may view each portion.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find interesting is that memory for agents has mostly been framed as an individual problem: one user, one agent, remembering preferences across sessions. But the hard and valuable version is at the team level. When you look at how a real engineering organization works, most of the knowledge that matters is not in the codebase. It is in people's heads, in Slack threads, in the reasoning behind a decision someone made two years ago. A new engineer spends months absorbing that before they are truly productive. Agents today start from zero every single time.

So the question becomes: how do you build a shared substrate where an agent working with one engineer learns something about how this team deploys services, or why a particular module is structured strangely, and that knowledge becomes available to every other agent on the team? Not as a static document, but as something that accumulates and gets corrected over time.

There are a few things that make this genuinely difficult. One is what to keep. If you store everything, you drown the agent in noise and it performs worse. If you are too selective, you lose the tacit stuff that was the whole point. Another is provenance and trust. If one engineer tells an agent "we never use this library," is that team policy or personal preference? A team-wide memory has to carry some notion of who said it and how confident to be. And then there is staleness. Codebases change constantly, and a memory that was true six months ago can actively mislead you today. You need mechanisms to verify and retire knowledge, not just add it.

What I think is exciting is that if you get this right, the agent becomes more like a long-tenured team member than a very capable contractor who shows up with amnesia every morning. And the compounding effect is real. Every interaction makes the system a little more useful for everyone else. That is a very different product dynamic from where most coding tools are today.

r001.rationale: The response discusses who contributed a memory and how much to trust it, but does not raise who is allowed to edit team-wide memory.

r002.rationale: The response describes memory as shared across agents but does not raise who may view different portions of it.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is: what should an individual agent learn that the whole team should then know? If one agent tries something and it fails, you’d like the other agents to avoid repeating that mistake. But you don’t necessarily want every detail of that attempt in every agent’s context. You want the useful lesson, along with enough context to know when it applies.

That makes memory more than a storage problem. It’s a problem of deciding what’s worth retaining, who needs it, and when it should be revised. An agent might conclude that a particular approach doesn’t work, but maybe it just used the wrong tool. If that conclusion becomes shared memory, you can turn one local mistake into a team-wide constraint.

So the thing I find compelling is the possibility of a team that gets better through working together. The test is whether one agent’s experience actually improves another agent’s next decision.

r001.rationale: The response asks what to retain, who needs it, and when to revise it, but does not raise who is allowed to edit team-wide memory.

r002.rationale: The response discusses which agents need useful lessons, but does not raise who may view different portions of memory as a design question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is: what should an agent learn from working with other agents? Having a shared place to put information is relatively straightforward. The hard part is deciding what belongs there, when to retrieve it, and when to stop trusting it.

Say one agent tries an approach and it fails. You’d like the rest of the team to benefit from that experience. But you don’t want them to conclude that the approach can never work, because the failure might have been specific to that task. So the memory needs to preserve enough context to make the lesson useful without turning every experience into a universal rule.

And then there’s this tension between sharing and attention. If every agent reads everything everyone else has done, you’ve created an enormous distraction. What you want is for the right experience to reach the right agent at the moment it changes a decision. That’s what makes it an interesting learning problem, beyond just a storage problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what information belongs in shared memory and how agents should learn from it, but does not raise who may edit that memory.

r002.rationale: The response discusses retrieving relevant experiences and avoiding distraction, but does not raise who may view different portions of the memory.
